body.text: China’s new strategic advantage is characterised as a chasm between broad public approval of AI in China and intensifying scepticism in the US. But what seems like an asset may be a misnomer and a cautionary tale.

Renowned French philosopher Michel Foucault argued that narratives shape what people believe and how they act on those beliefs. Theorising language’s influence on human behaviour, he argued that “power is tolerable only on condition that it mask a substantial part of itself”. Foucault reminds us to question what phrases like Chinese “enthusiasm” and American “doom” direct us to think and do.
AI may erode freedom of expression in the US if left to the prerogative of the Trump administration.

China additionally offers a dystopian preview of how AI can further curtail and pre-empt public expression. The government currently uses AI to scan and censor swathes of textual and visual data, while Chinese companies are developing technology that would allow the state to reshape public opinion through personalised propaganda and predict which individuals will become future dissidents.

However, while China’s access to public data has afforded it a scaling edge, it is the open-weight design that has made its models freely available, supporting its proliferation. Several approaches could allow US companies greater data access while preserving democracy and privacy. They include synthetic data generation, which creates information from algorithms and simulation models that mimic real-world scenarios. A lack of domestic debate and regulation would not offset the iterative advantage of China’s open models. It could unravel American democracy from the inside.

AI may erode freedom of expression in the US if left to the prerogative of the Trump administration, which has repeatedly violated the constitutional protection of free speech. Such a threat makes public debate surrounding AI a meta-safeguard for the very right to debate.

The Trump administration may also use digital tools to manipulate public opinion in elections, a tactic it employed – through human trolls – that predates the widespread and incisive competencies of AI. The risk of AI undermining free elections further underscores a need for public debate, which has animated both sides of the aisle.

Describing Chinese support for AI as the result of “optimism” and “enthusiasm” quietly counsel against such debate. Used to compare the US and China in what is characterised as a zero-sum race between the countries to dominate AI, these phrases suggest that the American public should surrender judgement calls surrounding regulatory guardrails. They imply that Americans’ concerns do not serve their self-interest. The irony of these descriptors lies in their exclusionary effects within the hawkish, binary framework of “us versus them”.

Given the Chinese government’s control over technology companies and their deployment of AI, “them” is clearly defined. “Us”, however, could mean tech executives who express societal aspirations for their R&D, politicians, civil society, or media in the United States. The appraisal of the American public’s concerns as a competitive disadvantage insinuates that the public should remove itself from decisions that will have significant political consequences.

Taking public pressure out of the equation may benefit AI executives and a White House that favours unilateral action. It is unlikely to benefit the American people, whose agency may be ephemeral as a result.
Sophie Berman is a researcher whose work focuses on the role of ethics in warfare, peace-making, and digital technologies. She holds an MPhil in International Relations from the University of Oxford.
